01.r: At that time he had not yet been born.
01.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse under 'of the past', usually with an imperfect verb, as here.

02.r: Gives the reason for what was just claimed about Levi.
02.n: The claim it explains is that of Hebrews 7:9: Levi gave the tenth through Abraham.

03.r: Inside his ancestor, as an unborn descendant.

04.r: Marks the loins of a particular man.

05.r: The body as the source of descendants.
05.n: Singular in Greek, 'loin'; English idiom says 'loins', and only the BSB keeps the singular. Abbott-Smith notes that the word is regarded, as by the Hebrews, as the seat of generative power, and cites this verse and Hebrews 7:5.

06.r: The article, here doing the work of 'his'; 'of' comes from the genitive case.
06.n: Literally 'of the father', as the YLT has it.

07.r: The forefather in whose body Levi still was: Abraham.
07.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is the male parent; here the word reaches back several generations, so the BSB writes 'ancestor' and the Geneva adds 'Abraham'. That Abraham is meant follows from the next clause, where Melchizedek meets him.

08.r: Levi, the subject carried over from what precedes.
08.n: The Greek leaves the subject inside the verb; the BSB names Levi. The imperfect describes a state that held at that time.

09.r: Sets the time: the meeting of Melchizedek and Abraham.

10.n: Abbott-Smith gives 'to meet with', with the person met in the dative, and cites this verse and Hebrews 7:1 for that use.

11.n: The BSB writes the name 'Abraham' for the pronoun.

13.n: Abbott-Smith gives the Hebrew form מַלְכִּי־צֶדֶק and notes that the Greek name does not change its ending.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus puts the article before the name, ὁ Μελχισεδέκ, 'the Melchizedek'. Greek often does this with names and English does not, so the difference does not show in the KJV.
